prompt: Explain how India measures forest cover and why the numbers need context.
hook: A map is not a tree.

card.oneLiner: India's forest and tree cover is assessed every two years by the Forest Survey of India, and it distinguishes satellite-observed forest cover from land that is legally a forest.
keyPoints: Changes are published in a biennial assessment report.
Forest cover is grouped by canopy density.
Tree cover outside forests is counted separately.
A rise in cover can coexist with a loss of quality forest.

framework.name: Forest Survey of India
framework.gloss: Biennial national assessment of forest and tree cover.

framework.name: Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change

whatYouCanDo: Look at density classes, not just the headline total.
Read the state and district tables for your area.
card.caveats: Educational information, not professional advice. Methodology and definitions matter when comparing years.

prompt: Explain the ecosystem services that forests provide.
hook: Forests are infrastructure you can breathe.

card.oneLiner: Forests store carbon, regulate water, cool the land and host biodiversity, providing services worth far more than their timber.
keyPoints: Trees absorb and store carbon dioxide.
Forests slow runoff and protect watersheds.
They moderate local temperature and humidity.
They support wildlife and rural livelihoods.

framework.name: IPCC AR6
framework.gloss: Forests as carbon sinks and their role in the land sector.

framework.name: Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change

whatYouCanDo: Value forests for services, not just land area.
card.caveats: Educational information, not professional advice. Valuing ecosystem services involves assumptions.

sources.title: Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change

prompt: Explain Project Tiger and how protecting a keystone species protects a forest.
hook: Saving one big cat saves a whole forest.

card.oneLiner: Project Tiger created a network of tiger reserves that protect the tiger and the ecosystem it depends on, from prey to prey's food.
keyPoints: It began in 1973 and now covers dozens of reserves.
Reserves have protected cores and buffer zones.
The tiger acts as an umbrella species for other wildlife.
Relocation and coexistence with communities are recurring issues.

framework.name: Project Tiger
framework.gloss: National tiger conservation programme and reserves.

framework.name: Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972
framework.gloss: Legal framework for national parks and sanctuaries.

whatYouCanDo: Support reserves as ecosystems, not tourist attractions.
Respect buffer-zone communities and their rights.
card.caveats: Educational information, not professional advice. Conservation approaches and outcomes vary by region.

prompt: Explain why wetlands matter and how they are protected.
hook: Wetlands are the kidneys of the landscape.

card.oneLiner: Wetlands filter water, absorb floods and support wildlife, and Ramsar sites and national rules protect them from filling and encroachment.
keyPoints: They store floodwater and recharge groundwater.
They filter pollutants and support rich biodiversity.
Designated Ramsar sites have international recognition.
Rules regulate activities such as filling and construction.

framework.name: Wetlands Rules, 2017
framework.gloss: National rules protecting wetlands and their boundaries.

whatYouCanDo: Identify wetlands in your city or district.
Oppose dumping and construction in wetland areas.
card.caveats: Educational information, not professional advice. Wetland protection varies in how it is enforced.

prompt: Explain invasive alien species and why they threaten native biodiversity.
hook: Some plants and animals are invaders.

card.oneLiner: Invasive alien species spread quickly, outcompete native species and can degrade forests and grasslands, so managing them is a conservation priority.
keyPoints: They arrive outside their natural range, often through trade or transport.
They spread fast and have few natural controls in the new range.
They can change fire, water and soil dynamics.
Management is costly and rarely fully successful.

framework.name: Convention on Biological Diversity
framework.gloss: Global commitments to prevent and control invasions.

framework.name: Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change

whatYouCanDo: Avoid releasing pets or plants into the wild.
Support native species in gardens and restoration.
Report unusual invasive growth to forest officials.
card.caveats: Educational information, not professional advice. Species considered invasive vary by region.
